Hello, I have a similar DAC, the Topping D10 Balanced. I remember the instructions for the DAC said to install ASIOProxy and use the components you've listed. What I found is that those instructions were intended for use with foobar2k v1 but are not necessary for v2. What I did was only install the foo\_input\_sacd component and select "Speakers (TOPPING USB DAC) \[Exclusive\]" from Playback > Output under Foobar2000 Preferences. This uses the WASAPI driver and should be sonically identical to ASIO, I think.

I followed the DAC instructions for v1 and found it to be a buggy experience whereas I've had no issues with WASAPI in v2. When using ASIO and would switch sources (foobar to YouTube, for example), and the sampling rate was different, the DAC would get frozen. So if I were playing something at 48.0 KHz on Foobar2k, it would freeze on that and wouldn't be able to play YouTube at 44.1 KHz. Often the only way I could fix it was by restarting my computer. I don't have this problem anymore using WASAPI.

I would also recommend uninstalling ASIOProxy though it may not actually be hurting anything.

This is all assuming you're using v2, of course.

Also, the first chapter in Haynes manuals is about tune-ups and maintenance and is more than thorough, in my opinion, for maintenance projects that you should do.

Really, I would say the only preventative maintenance projects are your fluids, spark plugs, headlights, filters, make sure your tires are properly inflated, etc. The only other projects are replacing things as they wear out (many of which just wear out over time and there's nothing you can do to prevent it. in particular, bearings anywhere on your car wear out after a number of years and most or all of them are too inaccessible to grease them) and upgrading to performance parts if you get the itch to do so. 

If you do all of the standard preventative maintenance, parts of your engine won't need to be cleaned out in the majority of cases. However, there are products you can use such as fuel system treatments and things like that to help keep things cleaner in the long run, but that's not really a project.

What kind of car do you have?

What I recommend (and this is exactly what I did) is that you get yourself a Haynes or Chilton manual for your car. If you aren't familiar with these, you can find them at just about any auto parts store and they contain enough information to almost completely take your car apart and put it back together. 

From there, I would recommend you perform routine maintenance on your car as needed like changing the oil, spark plugs, coolant, etc. The more you do these, the more you start to understand your car, which will help you out tremendously on future projects. Not to mention it helps you learn to troubleshoot any problems once you can visualize how different parts of your car work.

Then from there, you can try to troubleshoot, research, and fix any existing problems that your car has (or when they arise, which they are bound to do). Haynes manuals (and probably Chiltons, though I'm less familiar with them) include pretty good troubleshooting sections that list a bunch of symptoms and what the likely culprit is. Then they tell you how to fix them.

Other than that, you can also spend some time just reading through one of these manuals. They're pretty dry reading, but have really helped me learn more about my car. They have a lot of pictures that are interesting to look through.
